Jens Skjelderup
yens shel'der-oop
n. (bishop of Bergen, 1510–1582; removed the images and side altars from Bergen cathedral in 1570 against the merchants' protest)
From Danish Skjelderup, a place name; the given name Jens a northern form of John.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jens Skjelderup was a physician before he was a bishop, and he applied a surgeon's decision to the furniture of his cathedral. Appointed to Bergen in 1557, he found the church still full of medieval images, carved altars and the shrines the German merchants had endowed and continued to honour, and in 1570 he had them taken out. The German wharf complained loudly, sued, and appealed to Copenhagen; the king upheld the bishop. Skjelderup defended the act in writing on the ground of the second commandment and held the see until his death in 1582. The dictionary records him because the removal of images is the point at which Reformed conviction becomes visible and expensive, and because the usual objection, that the images were only reminders, was made to him and answered. The commandment does not distinguish between an image worshipped and an image merely kept for devotion: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4). The making is forbidden before the bowing is mentioned.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an image as a representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; graven as carved or engraved; and jealous as suspicious, and in Scripture emulous, requiring exclusive devotion.

expand to see more

IMAGE, n. [L. imago.] A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; a statue; a picture; an idol.

GRAVEN, participle passive. Carved; engraved; cut, as letters or figures, on a hard substance.

JEALOUS, adj. Suspicious that we do not enjoy the affection or respect of others; in Scripture, requiring exclusive devotion.

ALTAR, n. [L. altare.] A mount; an elevation of earth, stone or other material, on which sacrifices were offered.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

Exo 20:5 — "Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;"

Isa 42:8 — "I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images."

Psa 115:4 — "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands."

Modern Corruption

Physician turned bishop of Bergen, who stripped the cathedral of its images in 1570 and was sued by the German merchants for it.

expand to see more

The live corruption is the defence of religious imagery as pedagogy, the claim that a statue teaches the unlettered and is therefore permitted. Rome has made this argument since Gregory the Great and makes it still; the Eastern churches make a stronger version of it for icons and venerate them openly. The dictionary rejects both. Where images of God or of the saints stand in a place of worship, devotion attaches itself to them whatever the official distinction says, as the Bergen merchants' lawsuit demonstrated by the vehemence of their attachment.

The principle to recover is the second commandment entire, including its reason. God forbids the bowing as well as the making, “Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them” (Exo 20:5), and grounds the prohibition in His own jealousy. He will not share His glory with an artefact: “my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8). The psalmist reduces every such object to its materials and its maker, for “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4). Deuteronomy commanded Israel to deal with them physically, that “ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images” (Deu 7:5), and Hezekiah is commended because “He removed the high places, and brake the images” (2Ki 18:4).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pesel (H6459), a graven image; Hebrew qanna (H7067), jealous.

Usage

"“Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — the Bergen images removed, 1570."

"“my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8) — the German wharf sued and lost."

"“Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4) — held the see until his death in 1582."
